title: Ecclesiastes 5:8–20
context: The Preacher observes oppression within layers of officials, the restlessness of those who love money, and the grievous evil of hoarded wealth lost or left behind, since everyone departs as naked as he came. Against this he commends receiving food, drink, work, and the power to enjoy them as God’s gift and portion. Versification: English 5:8–20 is Hebrew 5:7–19; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the vanity of greed and joy received from God.

verses.text: If you see the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking away of justice and righteousness in a district, don’t marvel at the matter, for one official is eyed by a higher one, and there are officials over them.
verses.arminianNotes:
If you see the poor oppressed and justice violently taken away in a district, do not be surprised, for each official is watched by a higher one, with others above them. Oppression is layered.

Arminian readers see injustice honestly acknowledged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Interpreters differ on whether the hierarchy describes compounding corruption or a system of checks; the sense is not certain.

Reformed readers see human government as flawed under God’s rule. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not excuse oppression.

verses.text: Moreover the profit of the earth is for all. The king profits from the field.
verses.arminianNotes:
The profit of the land is for all, and the king himself profits from the field. Everyone depends on the earth’s produce.

Arminian readers see a reminder that rulers rely on ordinary labor.
verses.reformedNotes:
This verse is difficult, and translations render it in different ways; its connection with verse 8 is debated.

Reformed readers see all, high and low, dependent on God’s provision through the land. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the interpretation tentatively.

verses.text: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance, with increase. This also is vanity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Whoever loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, nor whoever loves abundance with increase; this also is vanity. Greed never has enough.

Arminian readers see the restlessness of a heart set on wealth.
verses.reformedNotes:
The saying exposes the emptiness of seeking fulfillment in money.

Reformed readers see the human heart restless when it seeks satisfaction apart from God. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about the vanity of greed and the futility of finding rest in possessions.

verses.text: When goods increase, those who eat them are increased; and what advantage is there to its owner, except to feast on them with his eyes?
verses.arminianNotes:
As goods increase, so do those who consume them, and the owner gains little but the sight of them. Wealth attracts dependents.

Arminian readers see the diminishing returns of accumulation, which often benefits others more than the one who gathered it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The owner may only ‘feast on them with his eyes.’ Possession does not equal enjoyment.

Reformed readers see the futility of trusting riches. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the limits of wealth and the burdens it brings with it.

verses.text: The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich will not allow him to sleep.
verses.arminianNotes:
The laborer’s sleep is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the rich man’s abundance keeps him awake. Simplicity can bring rest.

Arminian readers see contentment as a gift found in honest work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The contrast is between the rest of honest toil and the anxiety that wealth can bring.

Reformed readers see peace as God’s gift, not a product of possessions. Both traditions read this as shared ground about contentment and the anxieties that riches can create.

verses.text: There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher has seen a grievous evil under the sun: wealth hoarded by its owner to his harm. Riches can injure.

Arminian readers see the danger of choosing to cling to wealth rather than use it well and generously.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘under the sun’ marks the book’s focus on life as observed in this world.

Reformed readers see the self-destructive pull of greed. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the harm that hoarded wealth can bring to its owner.

verses.text: Those riches perish by misfortune, and if he has fathered a son, there is nothing in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Those riches are lost through misfortune, and if he has a son, nothing is left in his hand. Wealth can vanish suddenly.

Arminian readers see the uncertainty of riches, which can disappear before they can be passed on.
verses.reformedNotes:
The loss affects the next generation as well.

Reformed readers see God’s providence over gain and loss, which humbles human plans. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the instability of wealth and the folly of trusting in it as security for the future.

verses.text: As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
As he came naked from his mother’s womb, so he will go, taking nothing from his labor in his hand. Death strips all.

Arminian readers see a sobering call to hold possessions loosely.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image resembles Job 1:21, where Job also speaks of coming and returning naked. The thought is common to biblical wisdom.

Reformed readers see human dependence on God laid bare. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: This also is a grievous evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go. And what profit does he have who labors for the wind?
verses.arminianNotes:
This too is a grievous evil: as he came, so he goes, and what profit has he who labors for the wind? Toil ends empty.

Arminian readers see the question pressing readers to ask what labor is truly for.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘labors for the wind’ echoes the book’s recurring image of chasing wind.

Reformed readers see the futility of labor detached from God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the emptiness of toil pursued only for gain and the limits of what labor can secure.

verses.text: All his days he also eats in darkness, he is frustrated, and has sickness and wrath.
verses.arminianNotes:
All his days he eats in darkness, with frustration, sickness, and anger. The hoarder’s life is joyless.

Arminian readers see the inner cost of a life consumed by acquisition, which robs even daily meals of their pleasure.
verses.reformedNotes:
The picture is of a life without joy despite wealth.

Reformed readers see the misery of seeking life in riches rather than in God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the spiritual and emotional toll of greed, recorded honestly by the Preacher.

verses.text: Behold, that which I have seen to be good and proper is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, in which he labors under the sun, all the days of his life which God has given him; for this is his portion.
verses.arminianNotes:
What the Preacher has seen to be good is to eat, drink, and enjoy good in one’s labor all the days God gives, for this is one’s portion. Enjoyment is a gift.

Arminian readers see gratitude for ordinary gifts.
verses.reformedNotes:
The theme of eating and drinking as God’s gift recurs in the book (compare 2:24 and 3:13).

Reformed readers see contentment received from God’s hand. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about receiving life as God’s gift.

verses.text: Every man also to whom God has given riches and wealth, and has given him power to eat of it, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Whenever God gives riches and the power to enjoy them, to take one’s portion and rejoice in labor, this is God’s gift. The capacity to enjoy is itself given.

Arminian readers see God’s generosity received with thanks.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse distinguishes having wealth from being able to enjoy it, a contrast developed in 6:1–2.

Reformed readers see every good, including enjoyment, coming from God. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: For he shall not often reflect on the days of his life, because God occupies him with the joy of his heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
Such a person will not often brood over the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart. Joy displaces anxious reflection.

Arminian readers see God’s gift of joy lightening life’s burdens.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrasing is compact, but the joy is presented as God’s doing rather than the person’s achievement.

Reformed readers see joy as God’s gracious provision. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the sense hedged.
